Getting started with suest

Source: vignettes/suest.Rmd
suest.Rmd

suest() combines two or more separately fitted models so you can test whether predictions, marginal effects, or other quantities differ across the models. It supplies the joint robust covariance matrix those tests need, and leaves calculating and presenting the quantities themselves to marginaleffects.

Functions at a glance

  • suest() combines two or more fitted models and calculates their joint covariance matrix. Its twopart option combines the two parts of two-part models.
  • suest_newdata() stacks the models’ estimation samples, one block of rows per model.
  • suest_mi() pools suest() results across multiply imputed datasets.
  • The usual marginaleffects functions, including predictions(), avg_comparisons(), avg_slopes(), hypotheses(), and the plotting functions, work with the combined object, and modelsummary() makes tables from it.

Installation and setup 

remotes::install_github("tdmize/suest")
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)

Basic workflow

Two logit models of union membership, the second adding wages and work experience:

nlsw <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/nlsw88.dta"))
nlsw <- nlsw[!is.na(nlsw$union), ]
nlsw[c("collgrad", "south")] <- lapply(nlsw[c("collgrad", "south")], factor)

base <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south, family = binomial("logit"),
            data = nlsw)
adjusted <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south + wage + ttl_exp,
                family = binomial("logit"), data = nlsw)
combined <- suest(base, adjusted, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"))
combined
#> Seemingly Unrelated Estimation
#> Models: Base + Adjusted 
#> Model types: Base=logit, Adjusted=logit 
#> Model engines: Base=stats::glm, Adjusted=stats::glm 
#> Comparison scale: predicted probabilities 
#> Observations: Base=1,878, Adjusted=1,878 
#> Overlapping observations: 1,878 
#> Union observations: 1,878 
#> Parameters: 10
summary(combined)
#> 
#> Simultaneous results for Base, Adjusted                    Number of obs = 1,878
#> 
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>               |                 Robust
#>               | Coefficient  std. err.        z   P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
#> --------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------
#> Base          |
#>   (Intercept) |      -1.340      0.704   -1.903   0.057       -2.720       0.040
#>     collgrad1 |       0.507      0.119    4.246   0.000        0.273       0.741
#>           age |       0.009      0.018    0.519   0.604       -0.026       0.044
#>        south1 |      -0.747      0.116   -6.431   0.000       -0.974      -0.519
#> --------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------
#> Adjusted      |
#>   (Intercept) |      -1.761      0.719   -2.448   0.014       -3.171      -0.351
#>     collgrad1 |       0.311      0.132    2.356   0.018        0.052       0.570
#>           age |       0.008      0.018    0.428   0.668       -0.028       0.043
#>        south1 |      -0.677      0.118   -5.719   0.000       -0.909      -0.445
#>          wage |       0.054      0.014    3.820   0.000        0.026       0.081
#>       ttl_exp |       0.006      0.013    0.469   0.639       -0.020       0.032
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

effects <- avg_comparisons(combined, variables = "collgrad", newdata = nlsw)
effects
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  Base       0.0966     0.0238 4.07   <0.001 14.4 0.05006  0.143
#>  Adjusted   0.0574     0.0252 2.28   0.0227  5.5 0.00804  0.107
#> 
#> Term: collgrad
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
hypotheses(effects, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)   0.0392    0.00912 4.29   <0.001 15.8 0.0213 0.0571

The last command tests the difference between the two effects directly. That is different from checking whether one effect is statistically significant and the other is not.

Tests on coefficients

hypotheses() lists the coefficients of every model with their joint robust standard errors. b1, b2, … refer to them in that order, so they can be tested against each other across models:

hypotheses(combined)
#> 
#>                   Term Estimate Std. Error      z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  Base::(Intercept)     -1.33993     0.7041 -1.903   0.0570  4.1 -2.7199  0.0400
#>  Base::collgrad1        0.50691     0.1194  4.246   <0.001 15.5  0.2729  0.7409
#>  Base::age              0.00925     0.0178  0.519   0.6041  0.7 -0.0257  0.0442
#>  Base::south1          -0.74681     0.1161 -6.431   <0.001 32.9 -0.9744 -0.5192
#>  Adjusted::(Intercept) -1.76067     0.7193 -2.448   0.0144  6.1 -3.1705 -0.3508
#>  Adjusted::collgrad1    0.31130     0.1321  2.356   0.0185  5.8  0.0523  0.5703
#>  Adjusted::age          0.00778     0.0182  0.428   0.6684  0.6 -0.0278  0.0434
#>  Adjusted::south1      -0.67692     0.1184 -5.719   <0.001 26.5 -0.9089 -0.4449
#>  Adjusted::wage         0.05384     0.0141  3.820   <0.001 12.9  0.0262  0.0815
#>  Adjusted::ttl_exp      0.00615     0.0131  0.469   0.6387  0.6 -0.0195  0.0318
hypotheses(combined, hypothesis = "b2 = b6")
#> 
#>  Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>       b2=b6    0.196     0.0461 4.24   <0.001 15.5 0.105  0.286
hypotheses(combined, hypothesis = "(b2 - b6) / b2 = 0")
#> 
#>    Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (b2-b6)/b2=0    0.386      0.135 2.86  0.00419 7.9 0.122   0.65

Supported models

Single-level models

Model Fitted with
Linear regression lm()
Binary logit, probit, and complementary log-log glm(), glm2::glm2()
Ordered logit and probit MASS::polr(), ordinal::clm()
Multinomial logit nnet::multinom()
Poisson regression glm(), glm2::glm2()
Negative binomial regression MASS::glm.nb()
Constant-dispersion negative binomial (Stata’s nbreg, dispersion(constant)) glmmTMB::glmmTMB() with family = nbinom1()
Zero-inflated Poisson and negative binomial pscl::zeroinfl()
Other GLMs with identity, log, logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log links glm(), glm2::glm2()
Tobit regression censReg::censReg(); predictions are the latent mean
Interval, censored, and parametric survival regression survival::survreg() with a common scale
Gompertz and generalized gamma survival flexsurv::flexsurvreg() with dist = "gompertz" or "gengamma"
Truncated regression truncreg::truncreg()
Fractional response glm() with quasibinomial(): logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log link
Beta regression betareg::betareg() with a logit, probit, complementary log-log, or log-log link
Heteroskedastic probit and logit Rchoice::hetprob()
Bivariate probit GJRM::gjrm(), with the same or different predictors in each equation; mvProbit::mvProbit() with the same predictors
Instrumental-variable regression (two-stage least squares) fixest::feols(), unweighted and without absorbed fixed effects
Instrumental-variable probit Rchoice::ivpml(); predictions are average structural probabilities
Generalized ordered logit (gologit2), including partial proportional odds, with logit, probit, cloglog, log-log, or cauchit links VGAM::vglm() with cumulative(reverse = TRUE); for log-log, see Notes on specific models
Heckman selection (maximum likelihood) sampleSelection::selection(method = "ml")

Panel models

Model Fitted with
Linear fixed-, between-, and random-effects plm::plm() with individual effects
Random-effects logit and probit pglm::pglm(model = "random", effect = "individual")
Random-effects Poisson pglm::pglm(model = "random", effect = "individual", other = "sd")
Fixed-effects Poisson fixest::fepois(y ~ x | id)
Population-averaged (GEE) linear, logit, probit, complementary log-log, and Poisson geepack::geeglm() with independence, exchangeable, ar1, or unstructured correlation

Multilevel models

Model Fitted with
Linear, random intercept nlme::lme(method = "ML")
Linear (maximum likelihood) lme4::lmer(REML = FALSE)
Logit, probit, complementary log-log, and Poisson lme4::glmer(); with only a random intercept, any nAGQ

Except for nlme::lme(), these models can have random slopes, several of them, and a level nested in the grouping variable (three-level models); see Notes on specific models.

Combining models

Models can use the same, partially overlapping, or completely different samples. Any single-level models can be combined, including models for different outcomes and models for categorical outcomes. Results on different scales are labeled separately rather than treated as directly comparable.

Random-effects models (nlme::lme(), pglm(), glmmTMB(), lme4, clmm()) can be combined with each other, including different families, and with linear, logit, probit, complementary log-log, Poisson, negative binomial, and ordered logit and probit models, such as a logit model with a random-intercept logit model. They must be unweighted and share one grouping variable (for three-level models, the top level), and the system is clustered on that variable. Other panel models (plm(), geeglm()) can be combined only with models of the same kind.

Offsets work in most models, written in the formula or given in the offset argument. They are not supported in glmmTMB(), lme4, clmm(), pglm(), fixest::fepois(), VGAM::vglm(), flexsurv::flexsurvreg(), and GJRM::gjrm() models. Survey models need them in the formula, as offset().

A few models have settings worth knowing about; see Notes on specific models.

Different samples or groups

When the models are fitted to different samples, such as separate groups, each model’s effects are averaged over its own sample. That is the default when newdata is left out; newdata = suest_newdata(fit) says the same thing explicitly:

south_model <- glm(union ~ age + hours + collgrad, family = binomial("logit"),
                   data = nlsw, subset = south == 1)
nonsouth_model <- glm(union ~ age + hours + collgrad, family = binomial("logit"),
                      data = nlsw, subset = south == 0)
fit_groups <- suest(south_model, nonsouth_model,
                    model_names = c("South", "Non-South"))

effects_groups <- avg_comparisons(fit_groups, variables = "collgrad",
                                  newdata = suest_newdata(fit_groups))
effects_groups
#> 
#>      Group Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  South       0.0264     0.0316 0.837    0.402  1.3 -0.0355 0.0883
#>  Non-South   0.1341     0.0335 4.007   <0.001 14.0  0.0685 0.1998
#> 
#> Term: collgrad
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
hypotheses(effects_groups, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>             Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)   S  2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  (South) - (Non-South)   -0.108      0.046 -2.34   0.0193 5.7 -0.198 -0.0175

Cluster-robust standard errors

Supply a cluster variable to get cluster-robust standard errors for the combined models. The National Longitudinal Survey of Young Women follows the same women over many years, so the same two models of union membership, fitted to all the years, cluster on each woman’s ID:

nlswork <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/nlswork.dta"))

base_p <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south, family = binomial("logit"),
              data = nlswork)
adjusted_p <- glm(union ~ collgrad + age + south + ln_wage + ttl_exp,
                  family = binomial("logit"), data = nlswork)
fit_clustered <- suest(base_p, adjusted_p, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
                       cluster = "idcode")

effects_clustered <- avg_comparisons(fit_clustered, variables = "collgrad")
effects_clustered
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error      z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  Base      0.06226     0.0151  4.115   <0.001 14.7  0.0326 0.0919
#>  Adjusted -0.00436     0.0148 -0.294    0.768  0.4 -0.0333 0.0246
#> 
#> Term: collgrad
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
hypotheses(effects_clustered, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)   0.0666    0.00542 12.3   <0.001 112.9 0.056 0.0772

cluster takes one or more column names, or a list with one vector, matrix, or data frame matched to each model’s estimation sample. An observation that appears in more than one model must have the same cluster ID in each. Observations in completely different samples can belong to the same cluster, in which case the covariance between models can be nonzero.

Panel models cluster on the panel identifier by default. A cluster you supply must contain whole panels.

Probability weights

suest supports probability weights for linear, binary (logit, probit, complementary log-log), fractional, Poisson, negative binomial, ordered logit and probit, and multinomial logit models, and for other GLMs such as Gamma and quasi-Poisson models. Fit each model with weights =, and tell suest() that they are probability weights with weight_type = "pweight". wts = TRUE averages with the weights:

set.seed(376)
weighted <- data.frame(x = rnorm(500), z = rnorm(500))
weighted$mediator <- 0.5 * weighted$x - 0.3 * weighted$z + rnorm(500)
weighted$pw <- exp(0.2 * weighted$z + 0.1 * rnorm(500))
weighted$y <- 1 + 0.7 * weighted$x - 0.4 * weighted$z +
  0.6 * weighted$mediator + rnorm(500)

base_w <- lm(y ~ x + z, weights = pw, data = weighted)
adjusted_w <- lm(y ~ x + z + mediator, weights = pw, data = weighted)
fit_w <- suest(base_w, adjusted_w, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
               weight_type = "pweight")
fit_w
#> Seemingly Unrelated Estimation
#> Models: Base + Adjusted 
#> Model types: Base=lm, Adjusted=lm 
#> Model engines: Base=stats::lm, Adjusted=stats::lm 
#> Comparison scale: fitted values 
#> Weight type: pweight 
#> Observations: Base=500, Adjusted=500 
#> Overlapping observations: 500 
#> Union observations: 500 
#> Parameters: 9

effects_w <- avg_comparisons(fit_w, variables = "x", wts = TRUE)
effects_w
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  Base        1.003     0.0537 18.7   <0.001 255.9 0.898  1.108
#>  Adjusted    0.722     0.0480 15.0   <0.001 167.3 0.628  0.816
#> 
#> Term: x
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: +1
hypotheses(effects_w, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)    0.281     0.0322 8.74   <0.001 58.6 0.218  0.345

Weights must be positive and finite. An observation that appears in more than one model must have the same weight in each; weights can differ for observations in only one model, including completely different samples. When the models have different samples, wts = TRUE averages each model over its own sample with its own weights.

Survey data

suest supports the survey models in the table above, fitted from one common one-stage survey design, in any combination. Give suest() the design and a variable that identifies each observation. The example uses the stratified sample of California schools that comes with the survey package: does the effect of the percentage of English language learners on a school’s academic performance index shrink once the percentage of students eligible for free meals is held constant?

library(survey)
data(api)
design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, fpc = ~fpc,
                    data = apistrat)
base_s <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell, design)
adjusted_s <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals, design)
fit_survey <- suest(base_s, adjusted_s, model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted"),
                    survey_design = design, observation_id = "snum")

effects_survey <- avg_slopes(fit_survey, variables = "ell", wts = TRUE)
effects_survey
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  Base       -3.729      0.318 -11.7   <0.001 103.1 -4.35 -3.106
#>  Adjusted   -0.506      0.388  -1.3    0.192   2.4 -1.27  0.255
#> 
#> Term: ell
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: dY/dX
hypotheses(effects_survey, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)    -3.22      0.356 -9.06   <0.001 62.7 -3.92  -2.53

If a model uses a subset (domain) of the data, fit it to subset(design, ...) and still give suest() the full design. The joint covariance accounts for strata, primary sampling units, and one-stage finite population corrections. Replicate weights, multistage designs, calibration, and probability-proportional-to-size designs are not supported.

Multiple imputation

To combine results across imputed datasets, fit the same suest system in each one. With mice, with() does this, and marginaleffects functions then estimate within each imputation and pool the results with Rubin’s rules, including cross-model differences. The example imputes missing wages, education, and occupation in an extract of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), then asks whether the effect of education on wages is smaller once part-time work and occupation are held constant:

ah <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/addhealth4_mcar.dta"))
ah <- ah[c("wages", "edyrs", "woman", "age", "parttime", "occcat")]
ah$occcat <- factor(ah$occcat)
imp <- mice::mice(ah, m = 10, seed = 2307, printFlag = FALSE)

analyses <- with(imp, suest(
  lm(wages ~ edyrs + woman + age),
  lm(wages ~ edyrs + woman + age + parttime + occcat),
  model_names = c("Base", "Adjusted")
))
avg_comparisons(analyses, variables = "edyrs")
#> 
#>     Group Estimate Std. Error    t Pr(>|t|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %  Df
#>  Base         1.64     0.0996 16.5   <0.001 152.7  1.45   1.84 387
#>  Adjusted     1.45     0.1026 14.2   <0.001 130.6  1.25   1.66 663
#> 
#> Term: edyrs
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: +1
avg_comparisons(analyses, variables = "edyrs",
                hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise)
#> 
#>           Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    t Pr(>|t|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %  Df
#>  (Base) - (Adjusted)    0.188     0.0402 4.67   <0.001 17.0 0.108  0.267 120
#> 
#> Type: response

mice warns “Large sample assumed.” here. That is expected: suest reports large-sample statistics, so the pooled degrees of freedom are Rubin’s large-sample values.

suest_mi() pools the coefficients and their joint covariance:

pooled <- suest_mi(analyses)
summary(pooled)
#> 
#> Multiple-imputation estimates for Base, Adjusted           Number of obs = 4,307
#>                                                                 Imputations = 10
#>                                                     DF: min = 22.8, max = 1224.6
#> 
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>               | Coefficient  std. err.        t   P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
#> --------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------
#> Base          |
#>   (Intercept) |     -18.442      3.456   -5.336   0.000      -25.234     -11.651
#>         edyrs |       1.642      0.100   16.495   0.000        1.447       1.838
#>         woman |      -4.944      0.420  -11.781   0.000       -5.770      -4.118
#>           age |       0.500      0.109    4.591   0.000        0.286       0.714
#>         lnvar |       4.965      0.049  102.371   0.000        4.870       5.060
#> --------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------
#> Adjusted      |
#>   (Intercept) |     -12.534      3.649   -3.435   0.001      -19.710      -5.358
#>         edyrs |       1.455      0.103   14.176   0.000        1.253       1.656
#>         woman |      -5.013      0.478  -10.498   0.000       -5.956      -4.071
#>           age |       0.488      0.109    4.485   0.000        0.274       0.701
#>      parttime |       2.480      0.730    3.396   0.001        1.047       3.913
#>       occcat2 |      -2.099      0.850   -2.469   0.014       -3.773      -0.425
#>       occcat3 |      -6.310      1.061   -5.950   0.000       -8.394      -4.226
#>       occcat4 |      -1.330      1.339   -0.993   0.321       -3.958       1.298
#>       occcat5 |      -2.866      1.133   -2.529   0.012       -5.094      -0.638
#>       occcat6 |      -5.070      1.061   -4.777   0.000       -7.159      -2.982
#>       occcat7 |      -2.667      9.853   -0.271   0.789      -23.060      17.726
#>       occcat8 |      -5.040      1.117   -4.514   0.000       -7.239      -2.841
#>       occcat9 |      -4.810      0.883   -5.446   0.000       -6.547      -3.074
#>         lnvar |       4.944      0.048  102.361   0.000        4.849       5.039
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

marginaleffects functions give the same results on pooled as on analyses. A list of suest() results, one per imputation, or the result of with(mitools::imputationList(...), suest(...)) can also be passed to suest_mi(); marginaleffects then warns that it could not recover the original data from a mids object, which does not affect suest() results.
